passage.title: The Productivity Paradox
passage.text: When companies first sent their staff home during the pandemic, many managers predicted a collapse in productivity. What actually happened surprised almost everyone: output in many sectors rose. Freed from long commutes and constant interruptions, employees reported finishing tasks faster than ever. Yet three years on, a more complicated picture has emerged. Researchers at several universities have found that while individual productivity tends to stay high, innovation often suffers. Not only do remote teams hold fewer spontaneous conversations, but they also form fewer connections with colleagues outside their immediate group. It is precisely these informal exchanges, the researchers argue, that generate new ideas. Had companies measured creativity rather than simply counting completed tasks, they might have noticed the problem sooner. This does not mean that a full return to the office is the answer. Many workers who have tasted flexibility are unwilling to give it up, and firms that insist on five days a week risk losing their best people to competitors. Instead, the most successful organisations seem to be those that treat office time as something to be designed rather than demanded. They bring teams together on the same days, specifically for brainstorming and problem-solving, and leave focused individual work for home. In other words, the question is no longer where people work, but what kind of work each place is best suited for.

items.explanation: 'What actually happened surprised almost everyone: output in many sectors rose.'

passage.title: Farming on the Fortieth Floor
passage.text: In a converted warehouse on the edge of Singapore, rows of lettuce grow under purple LED lights, stacked twelve levels high. No soil is used; instead, the roots hang in a fine mist of water and nutrients. Supporters of vertical farming claim it could transform the way cities feed themselves. Because crops are grown indoors, they are protected from storms, droughts and pests, which means pesticides are unnecessary. Water use can be as much as ninety-five percent lower than in traditional agriculture, as moisture is captured and recycled. And since the farms can be built inside cities, food travels a few kilometres rather than hundreds. Critics, however, point to an awkward fact: the sun is free, but electricity is not. Lighting and climate control make vertical farms extremely energy-hungry, and unless that energy comes from renewable sources, the environmental benefits can largely disappear. Moreover, the technology currently works well only for leafy greens and herbs. Staple crops such as rice and wheat, which feed most of the world's population, need far more space and light, making them uneconomic to grow indoors. What seems likely, then, is that vertical farms will complement rather than replace conventional agriculture. For land-scarce cities like Singapore, which imports more than ninety percent of its food, even a modest increase in local production could make the food supply significantly more secure.

items.explanation: 'Because crops are grown indoors, they are protected from storms, droughts and pests, which means pesticides are unnecessary.'

passage.title: The Hidden Cost of Convenience
passage.text: With a few taps on a phone, you can order dinner, book a ride or have a sofa assembled in your living room within the hour. This convenience is made possible by the so-called gig economy, in which workers are paid per task rather than receiving a regular salary. For consumers, the arrangement is attractive: services are cheap, fast and available around the clock. For many workers, too, it offers genuine benefits. Students, carers and people with other jobs value the freedom to choose when and how much they work. Nevertheless, a growing body of evidence suggests that this flexibility comes at a price. Because gig workers are usually classified as independent contractors rather than employees, they are rarely entitled to sick pay, holidays or pensions. Their income can fluctuate dramatically from week to week, and algorithms, not human managers, often decide who gets offered work. Drivers in several countries have described being 'deactivated' from apps after receiving a handful of poor customer ratings, with little opportunity to appeal. Some governments have begun to respond. In 2021, Spain passed a law presuming that food-delivery riders are employees, while courts in the United Kingdom have ruled that certain drivers are entitled to the minimum wage. The challenge for lawmakers is to protect workers without destroying the flexibility that attracted so many of them in the first place.

items.explanation: They 'value the freedom to choose when and how much they work.'

passage.title: Why Lies Travel Faster
passage.text: A widely cited study of Twitter found that false news stories were seventy percent more likely to be shared than true ones and reached people up to six times faster. Perhaps surprisingly, the researchers concluded that automated accounts, or 'bots', were not mainly to blame. It was ordinary human users who spread the falsehoods. So why are we so drawn to misinformation? One explanation is novelty. False stories tend to be more surprising than the truth, and surprising information triggers strong emotions such as fear, anger or amazement. These emotions, in turn, make us more likely to hit 'share' before we have stopped to think. Another factor is identity. People are far more willing to accept a claim, however doubtful, if it confirms what they already believe about the world or flatters the group they belong to. What, then, can be done? Simply correcting false stories after they spread has limited effect, since corrections rarely travel as far as the original claim. A more promising approach, some psychologists argue, is 'prebunking': teaching people in advance about the techniques used to mislead, such as emotional language, fake experts and false choices. In one experiment, players of a short online game in which they created their own fake news became noticeably better at spotting misleading posts afterwards. Rather than telling people what to think, prebunking aims to help them recognise when someone is trying to manipulate them.

options: Automated accounts

Government agencies
items.explanation: 'It was ordinary human users who spread the falsehoods.'

passage.title: What Happens While We Sleep
passage.text: For centuries, sleep was regarded as little more than a period of rest, a necessary pause in which the body and mind simply switched off. Modern neuroscience has overturned this view entirely. Far from being inactive, the sleeping brain is engaged in a series of vital tasks, the most remarkable of which may be the consolidation of memory. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay the experiences of the day, transferring important information from the hippocampus, a short-term store, to the cortex, where it can be kept for the long term. This is why students who sleep after studying generally remember more than those who stay up all night revising. Sleep also seems to play a role in cleaning the brain. In 2013, scientists discovered that the spaces between brain cells expand during sleep, allowing fluid to wash away waste products that build up during the day, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. Worryingly, many people are not getting enough of it. Surveys suggest that around a third of adults in developed countries regularly sleep less than the recommended seven hours. Few of them realise that chronic sleep loss is associated not only with poor concentration but also with obesity, heart disease and depression. As one researcher put it, it is difficult to think of a single process in the body that is not improved by a good night's sleep.

passage.title: Less Is More?
passage.text: Three years ago, Hannah Clarke owned more than two hundred items of clothing, a car she rarely drove and a flat full of gadgets. Today, everything she owns fits into two suitcases. 'For families on low incomes, keeping things just in case is a perfectly rational strategy.' Others note the irony that minimalism has itself become a product, with books, apps and expensive designer furniture all marketed to those seeking a simpler life. Hannah acknowledges the criticism. 'Minimalism isn't about owning as little as possible,' she says. 'It's about owning things on purpose.'

passage.title: Too Many Visitors
passage.text: Every summer, the narrow streets of Venice fill with so many tourists that residents struggle to walk to the supermarket. The city's permanent population has fallen below fifty thousand, while it receives more than twenty million visitors a year. Venice is the most famous example of a phenomenon now known as overtourism, but it is far from the only one. From the beaches of Thailand to the mountain villages of Peru, popular destinations are struggling to cope with the sheer number of people who want to see them. The causes are not hard to identify. Cheap flights, cruise ships and social media have made travel more accessible than ever, while photo-sharing apps encourage millions of people to visit exactly the same spots in search of the same picture. The consequences, however, are serious. Rents rise as flats are converted into holiday rentals, forcing local people out of city centres. Fragile environments are damaged, and traditional shops are replaced by souvenir stalls. In response, some places have introduced bold measures. Venice now charges day-trippers an entrance fee on busy days, Amsterdam has banned new hotels in its centre, and Thailand's Maya Bay, made famous by a Hollywood film, was closed entirely for several years to allow its coral reefs to recover. Such measures are controversial, since tourism also provides jobs and income. Yet unless destinations manage visitor numbers carefully, they risk destroying the very qualities that made them attractive in the first place.

passage.title: The Last Speakers
passage.text: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around half could disappear by the end of this century. Many are spoken by only a few hundred people, most of them elderly, and some by just a single person. When a language dies, it is not only words that are lost. Each language contains a unique way of seeing the world: knowledge of local plants and medicines, systems for describing family relationships, songs and stories that have been passed down orally for generations. Some Aboriginal Australian languages, for example, use compass directions rather than words like 'left' and 'right', so speakers are constantly aware of where north is. Languages usually decline when a community comes under pressure to adopt a more dominant language, often for economic reasons. Parents may stop speaking their mother tongue to their children in the belief that another language will offer them better opportunities. Within a couple of generations, the original language can vanish. Yet the story is not entirely one of loss. Welsh, which was in steep decline in the twentieth century, is now spoken by more young people than it was fifty years ago, thanks largely to Welsh-language schools and television. Even more remarkably, Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language after nearly two thousand years in which it was used mainly in religious texts. These examples suggest that, with enough commitment, endangered languages can be saved.

items.explanation: It illustrates that 'each language contains a unique way of seeing the world'.

passage.title: Who Owns AI Art?
passage.text: In 2022, a picture created with an artificial intelligence program won first prize in the digital art category of a state fair in Colorado. The man who entered it had typed a series of text instructions, or 'prompts', into the software and then edited the results. His victory provoked an angry reaction from many artists, who argued that he had not really created anything at all. The controversy raised a question that courts and governments are still struggling to answer: who, if anyone, owns a work produced by AI? In the United States, the Copyright Office has so far refused to protect images generated entirely by machines, arguing that copyright requires human authorship. However, it has indicated that works combining AI output with significant human creativity may qualify. Other countries have taken different positions, and the law is changing rapidly. A second, equally heated debate concerns the data used to train these systems. AI image generators learn by analysing millions of pictures collected from the internet, many of them created by professional artists who were neither asked for permission nor paid. Several artists have taken legal action, claiming that their work has been used without consent to build products that now compete with them. Technology companies respond that the AI does not copy images but learns general patterns, much as a human art student learns by studying the old masters. How this argument is settled could shape the creative industries for decades to come.

passage.title: Who Owns AI Art?
passage.text: In 2022, a picture created with an artificial intelligence program won first prize in the digital art category of a state fair in Colorado. The man who entered it had typed a series of text instructions, or 'prompts', into the software and then edited the results. His victory provoked an angry reaction from many artists, who argued that he had not really created anything at all. The controversy raised a question that courts and governments are still struggling to answer: who, if anyone, owns a work produced by AI? In the United States, the Copyright Office has so far refused to protect images generated entirely by machines, arguing that copyright requires human authorship. However, it has indicated that works combining AI output with significant human creativity may qualify. Other countries have taken different positions, and the law is changing rapidly. A second, equally heated debate concerns the data used to train these systems. AI image generators learn by analysing millions of pictures collected from the internet, many of them created by professional artists who were neither asked for permission nor paid. Several artists have taken legal action, claiming that their work has been used without consent to build products that now compete with them. Technology companies respond that the AI does not copy images but learns general patterns, much as a human art student learns by studying the old masters. passage.title: The Four-Day Week Experiment
passage.text: In 2022, around seventy British companies took part in what was then the world's largest trial of a four-day working week. Employees worked eighty percent of their usual hours for one hundred percent of their pay, on the condition that they maintained at least the same level of output. The results, published six months later, were striking. The vast majority of companies chose to continue with the new schedule, and several made it permanent. Staff reported lower levels of stress and burnout, better sleep and more time for family and hobbies. Crucially for employers, revenue remained broadly stable, while the number of staff leaving fell significantly. How was this possible? Many firms found that a large proportion of the working week had been wasted on unnecessary meetings, unclear priorities and constant email. Forced to fit their work into four days, teams cut meetings shorter, introduced periods of uninterrupted 'focus time' and became more disciplined about what really mattered. Sceptics, however, urge caution. The companies involved had volunteered for the trial, so they were probably more enthusiastic than average. Moreover, most were in office-based sectors such as marketing and finance. Whether the model could work in hospitals, schools or factories, where output depends on the number of hours people are physically present, remains an open question. Even so, the trial has shifted the debate. The idea of a shorter working week, once dismissed as unrealistic, is now being seriously discussed by governments and businesses worldwide.

passage.title: The Invisible Pollution
passage.text: Plastic pollution used to conjure up images of bottles floating in the ocean or turtles tangled in fishing nets. Increasingly, though, scientists are concerned about something far harder to see. Microplastics, fragments smaller than five millimetres, have now been found almost everywhere researchers have looked: in Arctic ice, on the summit of Mount Everest, in drinking water and even in human blood. Some are manufactured deliberately, such as the tiny beads once common in face scrubs. Most, however, are produced when larger items break down, or are released from synthetic clothing every time it is washed. A single load of laundry can shed hundreds of thousands of fibres, many of which pass through water treatment plants and end up in rivers and seas. What these particles are doing to our health is still unclear. Laboratory studies have shown that microplastics can cause inflammation in human cells, and some carry chemicals that interfere with hormones. But laboratory conditions are very different from everyday exposure, and scientists stress that more research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn. Meanwhile, some practical steps are already being taken. Several countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics, and France will require all new washing machines to be fitted with microfibre filters. Individuals can contribute too, by washing clothes less often, at lower temperatures and in fuller loads. None of these measures will solve the problem on its own, but together they could significantly reduce the amount of plastic entering the environment.

passage.title: Why We Put Things Off
passage.text: Almost everyone procrastinates from time to time, but for some people, delaying important tasks becomes a serious problem that damages their studies, careers and health. For a long time, procrastination was regarded as a sign of laziness or poor time management. Psychologists now believe that this explanation misses the point. According to Dr Tim Pychyl, who has studied the subject for over twenty years, procrastination is primarily an emotional problem rather than a practical one. We avoid tasks not because we cannot organise our time, but because the task makes us feel bad: bored, anxious, frustrated or afraid of failure. Putting it off brings immediate relief, which is why the habit is so difficult to break. The relief, of course, is temporary. As the deadline approaches, stress increases, and the task often becomes even more unpleasant than it would have been. Understanding procrastination in this way suggests different solutions. Rather than buying another planner, people are advised to focus on how they feel. One effective technique is simply to start with a very small step, such as writing a single sentence or opening the relevant document. Once we have begun, the task usually turns out to be less unpleasant than we feared. Another is self-compassion. Studies have found that students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next. Criticising ourselves, it seems, only adds to the negative feelings that caused the delay in the first place.

options: It is now considered helpful.

items.explanation: '…procrastination is primarily an emotional problem rather than a practical one.'

passage.title: Volunteering Abroad: Help or Harm?
passage.text: Each year, hundreds of thousands of young people from wealthy countries pay to spend a few weeks volunteering in developing nations, building schools, teaching English or caring for children in orphanages. The industry, sometimes called 'voluntourism', is worth an estimated two billion dollars annually. On the surface, it seems to benefit everyone: volunteers gain experience and a sense of purpose, while communities receive help they badly need. A closer look, however, reveals some uncomfortable truths. Many volunteers have no relevant skills, and a school built by inexperienced teenagers may need to be rebuilt by local workers once they have left, which is hardly an efficient use of resources. Such projects can also take paid work away from local people. Most troubling of all is orphanage tourism. Research in countries such as Cambodia and Nepal has found that the majority of children living in orphanages have at least one living parent. Some institutions deliberately keep children in poor conditions in order to attract donations from visitors, and the constant arrival and departure of short-term volunteers can harm children's emotional development. This is not to say that all international volunteering is harmful. Experts suggest that the best programmes are those that are led by local organisations, match volunteers' skills to genuine needs and last long enough to make a real difference. A qualified nurse spending six months training local health workers, for example, is likely to achieve far more than a student spending two weeks painting a classroom.

It is built in the wrong place.
items.explanation: '…may need to be rebuilt by local workers once they have left, which is hardly an efficient use of resources.'

passage.title: Volunteering Abroad: Help or Harm?
passage.text: Each year, hundreds of thousands of young people from wealthy countries pay to spend a few weeks volunteering in developing nations, building schools, teaching English or caring for children in orphanages. The industry, sometimes called 'voluntourism', is worth an estimated two billion dollars annually. On the surface, it seems to benefit everyone: volunteers gain experience and a sense of purpose, while communities receive help they badly need. A closer look, however, reveals some uncomfortable truths. Many volunteers have no relevant skills, and a school built by inexperienced teenagers may need to be rebuilt by local workers once they have left, which is hardly an efficient use of resources. Such projects can also take paid work away from local people. Most troubling of all is orphanage tourism. Research in countries such as Cambodia and Nepal has found that the majority of children living in orphanages have at least one living parent. Some institutions deliberately keep children in poor conditions in order to attract donations from visitors, and the constant arrival and departure of short-term volunteers can harm children's emotional development. This is not to say that all international volunteering is harmful. Experts suggest that the best programmes are those that are led by local organisations, match volunteers' skills to genuine needs and last long enough to make a real difference. A qualified nurse spending six months training local health workers, for example, is likely to achieve far more than a student spending two weeks painting a classroom.

passage.title: Science for Everyone
passage.text: In 2007, a Dutch schoolteacher named Hanny van Arkel was looking through images of galaxies on a website when she noticed a strange green cloud that nobody had seen before. Her discovery, now known as 'Hanny's Voorwerp' (Dutch for 'object'), turned out to be a rare type of glowing gas and became the subject of numerous scientific papers. Van Arkel was not a professional astronomer. She was one of hundreds of thousands of volunteers taking part in Galaxy Zoo, a project that invited members of the public to help classify galaxies photographed by telescopes. This kind of collaboration, known as citizen science, has grown rapidly in recent years. Volunteers now count birds, record the timing of spring flowers, transcribe historical documents and even play online puzzle games that help researchers understand how proteins fold. The advantages for science are obvious. Projects can gather far more data than any research team could manage alone, and human beings remain better than computers at certain tasks, particularly recognising unusual patterns. For participants, the rewards include learning new skills and the satisfaction of contributing to real research. Nevertheless, citizen science has its limitations. Data collected by untrained volunteers can be inconsistent, so projects must include careful checks, such as having several people classify the same image. There is also a risk that volunteers are treated simply as free labour. The most successful projects, therefore, are those that keep participants informed about the results and give them proper credit for their contributions.

passage.title: The Power of Belief
passage.text: In medical trials, new drugs are usually tested against a placebo: a pill that looks identical but contains no active ingredient. Patients do not know which one they are taking, so any difference in results can be attributed to the drug itself. What is remarkable is how often patients taking the placebo also improve. For conditions such as pain, depression and irritable bowel syndrome, placebos can produce significant benefits, sometimes almost as large as those of the real treatment. This phenomenon, known as the placebo effect, is not simply imagination. Brain scans have shown that when people expect pain relief, their brains release natural painkillers called endorphins. Expectations, in other words, can trigger real physical changes. The context also matters. Studies have found that expensive placebos work better than cheap ones, injections better than pills, and that a doctor who is warm and confident produces better outcomes than one who is cold and distracted. Perhaps most surprising of all is the 'open-label' placebo. In several experiments, patients were told honestly that they were receiving sugar pills with no active ingredient, yet many still reported feeling better. Researchers suggest that the ritual of taking a pill, combined with the attention of a caring professional, may be enough to activate the body's own healing mechanisms. None of this means that placebos can cure serious diseases such as cancer. But it does suggest that the way treatment is delivered may be almost as important as the treatment itself.

passage.title: The Myth of Multitasking
passage.text: Many of us are proud of our ability to multitask: answering emails during meetings, texting while watching television or listening to podcasts while studying. Yet research consistently shows that, for most tasks, the human brain is simply not capable of doing two things at once. What we call multitasking is really task-switching, as attention moves rapidly back and forth between activities. Each switch carries a cost. It takes time for the brain to refocus, and errors increase as we try to pick up where we left off. Some estimates suggest that frequent switching can reduce productivity by as much as forty percent. Even more worrying is research from Stanford University, which found that people who regularly multitask with digital media performed worse on tests of attention and memory than those who rarely did. Contrary to what one might expect, the heavy multitaskers were more easily distracted by irrelevant information, not less. It is unclear whether multitasking causes these difficulties or whether people who are already easily distracted are more likely to multitask, but either way, the habit does not seem to be doing us any favours. There are exceptions. We can combine an automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one, such as having a conversation. Problems arise when two tasks compete for the same mental resources, which is why talking on the phone while driving is so dangerous, even with a hands-free device. For tasks that require real concentration, the advice is clear: do one thing at a time.

What we call multitasking is really task-switching, as attention moves rapidly back and forth between activities. Each switch carries a cost. It takes time for the brain to refocus, and errors increase as we try to pick up where we left off. Some estimates suggest that frequent switching can reduce productivity by as much as forty percent. Even more worrying is research from Stanford University, which found that people who regularly multitask with digital media performed worse on tests of attention and memory than those who rarely did. Contrary to what one might expect, the heavy multitaskers were more easily distracted by irrelevant information, not less. It is unclear whether multitasking causes these difficulties or whether people who are already easily distracted are more likely to multitask, but either way, the habit does not seem to be doing us any favours. There are exceptions. We can combine an automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one, such as having a conversation. Problems arise when two tasks compete for the same mental resources, which is why talking on the phone while driving is so dangerous, even with a hands-free device. For tasks that require real concentration, the advice is clear: do one thing at a time.

passage.title: Robots in the Care Home
passage.text: Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world: almost thirty percent of its citizens are over sixty-five, and the country faces a severe shortage of care workers. In response, the government has invested heavily in robots designed to help look after elderly people. Some are practical, such as machines that lift patients out of bed, reducing back injuries among staff. Others are intended to provide companionship. Paro, a soft robotic seal that responds to touch and sound, has been used in care homes for years, and studies suggest it can reduce stress and loneliness in people with dementia. Supporters argue that robots could allow human carers to spend less time on physically exhausting tasks and more time on meaningful interaction. However, the technology has spread more slowly than expected. A study of care homes that introduced robots found that many devices were abandoned within a few months, as they proved difficult to operate, required constant maintenance or simply did not fit into daily routines. Some staff felt that the robots created extra work rather than saving time. There are ethical concerns, too. Critics worry that robots might become a cheap substitute for human contact, leaving vulnerable people more isolated rather than less. Others question whether it is acceptable to give people with dementia a machine that they may believe is a real animal. Most experts agree that robots can play a useful supporting role, but few believe they will ever replace the warmth and judgement of a human carer.

passage.title: Gardening Under the Sea
passage.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species and provide food and income for hundreds of millions of people. They are also among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change. When sea temperatures rise even slightly above normal for several weeks, corals expel the tiny algae that live inside them and give them their colour. This process, known as bleaching, leaves the coral white and, if conditions do not improve, eventually kills it. Australia's Great Barrier Reef has suffered several mass bleaching events since 2016. Faced with this crisis, scientists and volunteers around the world have begun to act as underwater gardeners. In coral nurseries, small fragments of healthy coral are grown on frames or ropes until they are large enough to be transplanted onto damaged reefs. Some researchers are going further, selecting and breeding corals that can tolerate higher temperatures, an approach sometimes described as 'assisted evolution'. Results so far have been encouraging on a local scale, with restored areas showing a return of fish and other marine life. Yet the scientists involved are the first to admit the limitations of their work. Restoration is slow and expensive, and the areas that can be replanted are tiny compared with the vast size of the world's reefs. As one marine biologist put it, restoration can buy time, but it cannot save the reefs unless global carbon emissions are dramatically reduced.

passage.title: Is Gaming a Sport?
passage.text: When a stadium in Seoul sold out for the final of a video game tournament, with tens of thousands of fans cheering and millions more watching online, it was clear that competitive gaming had become more than a hobby. Esports, as it is known, now attracts global audiences of around half a billion people, and top players can earn millions of dollars in prize money and sponsorship. Esports even made its debut as an official medal event at the 2022 Asian Games. Yet the question of whether gaming should be considered a sport remains hotly debated. Supporters point out that professional gamers train for up to ten hours a day, need lightning-fast reactions and sophisticated strategic thinking, and must cope with intense pressure in front of huge crowds. Research has found that elite players can perform several hundred precise actions per minute, a level of fine motor skill comparable to that of a concert pianist. They also argue that chess, which involves even less physical movement, has long been recognised as a sport in many countries. Opponents are not persuaded. For them, sport necessarily involves significant physical exertion, and sitting in a chair, however skilfully, does not qualify. Others raise concerns about health, pointing to cases of repetitive strain injuries and burnout among young players, many of whom retire before the age of twenty-five. Whatever the answer, one thing is certain: with audiences and investment still growing, esports is not going away.
